item.title: Putting a Rare Vaccine-Related Adverse Event into Context-Shouldering a Small Risk
Risk of Shoulder Injury Related to Vaccine Administration for COVID-19 and Influenza Vaccinations
item.description:
Importance: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine identified a critical evidence gap regarding the risk of shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA) after COVID-19 vaccination.

Objective: To compare the risk of SIRVA after COVID-19 vs influenza vaccinations in adults.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based cohort study included individuals aged at least 18 years who received a COVID-19 or influenza vaccination administered via intramuscular deltoid injection between August 1, 2023, and April 30, 2024, at Kaiser Permanente Southern California. Data were analyzed from June 2024 to September 2026.

Exposure: Receipt of COVID-19 vaccination or influenza vaccination.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was incident SIRVA, defined as shoulder symptoms beginning at or before 7 days and persisting more than 30 days after vaccination, identified using a validated natural language processing algorithm. Incidences were calculated per 10 000 vaccinations. Adjusted relative risks (RRs), risk differences, and 95% CIs were estimated using robust Poisson regression with inverse probability of treatment weighting.

Results: A total of 1 366 362 individuals (mean [SD] age at vaccination, 58.4 [18.2] years; 782 994 female [57.3%]) across 1 901 588 vaccinations were included (1 076 609 vaccinations [56.7%] were administered to females). Among 1 830 636 vaccinations in the primary analysis, 252 SIRVA cases were identified as follows: 110 cases (0.018%) after 596 614 COVID-19 vaccinations and 142 cases (0.012%) after 1 234 022 influenza vaccinations. An additional 13 SIRVA cases (0.018%) were identified among 70 952 simultaneous COVID-19 and influenza vaccinations. Most COVID-19 vaccines were Pfizer-BioNTech messenger RNA (667 455 of 667 566 [99.98%]), and influenza vaccines were predominantly standard-dose (866 530 of 1 304 974 [66.40%]) or high-dose (438 183 of 1 304 974 [33.58%]) inactivated quadrivalent formulations. SIRVA incidence was higher after COVID-19 than influenza vaccination, at an incidence of 1.84 (95% CI, 1.53-2.22) vs 1.15 (95% CI, 0.98-1.36) per 10 000 vaccinations, corresponding to an adjusted absolute increase of 0.67 cases (95% CI, 0.15-1.19) per 10 000 vaccinations (adjusted RR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.16-2.28). Among adults 65 years or older, SIRVA incidence was 2.11 (95% CI, 1.67-2.67) per 10 000 for COVID-19 vaccination and 1.63 (95% CI, 1.28-2.07) per 10 000 for high-dose influenza vaccination (adjusted RR, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.92-2.15).

Conclusions and relevance: Results of this cohort study suggest that although SIRVA was rarely associated with both vaccines, COVID-19 vaccination was associated with approximately 7 additional cases per 100 000 vaccinations compared with influenza vaccination. Among adults aged 65 years or older, SIRVA risk did not differ significantly between COVID-19 and high-dose influenza vaccination. The small absolute risk of SIRVA should be considered alongside the established benefits of COVID-19 and influenza vaccination in preventing severe disease and hospitalization.

Zheng C, Qian L, Sy LS, Goodwin GV, Yeh M, Navarro RA

item.title: Surveillance Mammography and Second Primary Breast Cancer Diagnosis Among Older Women With a History of Breast Cancer
item.description:
Importance: Although surveillance mammography is commonly performed among older women, whether this practice improves clinical outcomes in this population is uncertain.

Objective: To evaluate the association between surveillance mammography and second primary breast cancer stage at diagnosis among older women with a history of breast cancer.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective longitudinal cohort study used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program-Medicare data. Women with nonmetastatic breast cancer that was diagnosed from 2004 to 2008 at 67 years or older who had a surveillance mammogram at approximately 5 years after diagnosis were included. Analyses used cause-specific hazard models with inverse probability of treatment weighting to estimate the risk of stage-specific second primary breast cancer among women who continued surveillance mammography and those who did not. Analyses were stratified by hormone receptor (HR) status of the initial breast cancer. Follow-up continued until second breast cancer diagnosis, death, or end of the study (December 2021). Analyses were performed between November 2025 and August 2026.

Exposure: Continued surveillance mammography more than 5 years after initial diagnosis.

Main outcomes and measures: Stage-specific cumulative incidence of a second primary breast cancer, categorized as in situ, localized, or advanced (regional or distant).

Results: Among 9888 women (mean [SD] age, 81.1 [5.5] years; 387 Hispanic [3.9%], 514 non-Hispanic Black [5.1%], and 8514 White individuals [86.1%]), 8055 (81.4%) had in situ or localized disease and 7621 (76.9%) had HR-positive tumors at initial diagnosis. Overall, 7940 women (80.3%) continued surveillance at cohort entry. Advanced second primary breast cancer was rare, and incidence did not differ among those who continued surveillance and those who did not (cumulative incidence, 1.65% vs 2.15%; hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.46-1.26). Results were similar in subgroups of women with initial HR-positive and HR-negative breast cancer.

Conclusions and relevance: The results of this cohort study suggest that among older survivors of breast cancer, continued surveillance mammography was not associated with a reduced risk of advanced second primary breast cancer. The absolute risk of advanced cancer was low, and surveillance decisions should be individualized given the potential burdens of continued surveillance.

Richman IB, Long JB, Lindsay ME, Sheffrin M, Berger ER
